title: Private Capex in India: Why Corporate Tax Cuts Cannot Replace Wage Growth
summary: Private capex in India remains sluggish despite corporate tax cuts, as stagnant rural wages and weak consumption keep factory capacity utilisation below 75%.

# Private Capex in India: Why Corporate Tax Cuts Cannot Replace Wage Growth


Record corporate profits and tax windfalls cannot ignite fresh investment when stagnant wages throttle consumer demand and leave factory capacity idling.


Indian Economy, Planning, Mobilization Of Resources, Growth, Development And Employment


Government Budgeting


Investment Models


Changes In Industrial Policy And Effects On Industrial Growth


Nov, 2026


•


9 min read


India's capital formation challenge centers on activating private corporate investments alongside sovereign infrastructure spending.


### Overview


India’s persistent private investment drought shows that supply-side tax concessions cannot replace household purchasing power. When aggregate demand stalls due to prolonged real wage stagnation across rural and informal labour markets, cutting corporate levies fails to spark factories.


Following the steep reductions under the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019, corporate balance sheets saw record profitability and substantial **balance-sheet deleveraging** . Yet, private sector Gross Fixed Capital Formation failed to stage a durable recovery because industrial capacity utilisation hovered near 74.6%, safely below the threshold required to trigger broad-based greenfield capital outlays. Sustained capital formation requires an **accelerator effect** powered by mass consumption, demanding a policy rebalance toward wage growth, rural safety nets, and formal employment.


## Why in the News: The Missing Relay Baton in India's Investment Cycle


The Union Government has repeatedly urged corporate India to accelerate private capital expenditure to relieve sovereign fiscal pressures. Addressing the centenary convention and 100th Annual General Meeting of FICCI on November 19, 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi publicly pulled up corporate leaders for keeping wages static and failing to expand employment despite receiving substantial corporate tax cuts.


This public critique followed earlier expressions of official frustration:


- In September 2022, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman likened corporate India's hesitancy to invest to **Lord Hanuman needing a reminder** of his strength at the Mindmine Summit.
- By late 2026, the expected transition from public-led infrastructure expansion to self-sustaining private investment had failed to materialise.


The Central Government scaled public capital outlays to **₹11.11 lakh crore** in FY 2024-25 and maintained annual capital budgets around ₹11-12 lakh crore in subsequent fiscal years to support gross domestic output. Yet, corporate capital formation has not picked up the relay baton, leaving the macroeconomic growth engine excessively reliant on sovereign borrowing.


Statutory reductions under the 2019 corporate tax overhaul resulted in Personal Income Tax collections surpassing Corporate Income Tax receipts.


## The 2019 Corporate Tax Bet: What Was Promised vs What Corporates Delivered


The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 overhauled India's corporate fiscal framework to kickstart an investment cycle. The statute introduced two concessional tax regimes under the Income-tax Act, 1961:


- **Section 115BAA:** Reduced the headline corporate tax rate for existing domestic firms to **22%** , conditional on foregoing designated exemptions.
- **Section 115BAB:** Cut the corporate tax rate for newly established manufacturing units to **15%** , subject to similar exemption trade-offs.


Supply-side theory presumed that lowering corporate taxation would unlock retained earnings and stimulate immediate greenfield outlays. According to a Press Information Bureau release by the Ministry of Finance, the annual revenue foregone from these tax cuts and associated relief measures stood at approximately **₹1.45 lakh crore** .


Rather than accelerating industrial expansion, this concession triggered a structural shift in direct tax composition:


- **Shift in revenue balance:** Time-series data released by the Central Board of Direct Taxes indicates that **Personal Income Tax collections surpassed** Corporate Income Tax collections following the 2019 statutory amendments.
- **Subdued capex recovery:** Despite the state surrendering considerable direct tax revenues, Gross Fixed Capital Formation by the private corporate sector has hovered around **10-11% of GDP** , remaining well below its historical peak of 14-16% recorded in 2007-08 and 2011-12.

## Profits Without Factories: How Tax Windfalls Went to Debt Paydown and Dividends


Corporate balance sheets absorbed the fiscal windfalls to bolster solvency rather than expanding physical plant capacity. According to a thematic study published in the Reserve Bank of India Bulletin examining listed non-government non-financial companies, post-pandemic corporate earnings and tax savings were deployed into three primary avenues rather than fresh greenfield physical assets:


- Rapid **balance sheet deleveraging** and debt servicing;
- Liquid cash accumulation and treasury investments; and
- Higher dividend payouts and equity buybacks.


Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran highlighted this disconnect, noting that while corporate profits of listed entities compounded at over **30% post-pandemic** , the rate of private sector capital formation failed to mirror that corporate profitability. Corporate boards responded rationally to existing incentives. Without steady consumer off-take, retiring debt and holding liquid assets was safer than erecting unneeded physical factories.


Private investment intentions documented by the Reserve Bank of India show that while bank-sanctioned project proposals rose to **₹4.4 lakh crore** in 2025-26, ground-level completion and execution remained cautious due to external demand volatility. Corporate managers deferred major capital outlays, waiting for clear signals of sustained final demand before committing capital to irreversible physical projects.


Corporate earnings following tax cuts were predominantly channeled into debt reduction and cash reserves rather than new physical plants.


## The Capacity Trap: Why Stagnant Rural Wages Cap Factory Utilization


Factory investment stalls when existing machines sit idle. Round 74 of the RBI Order Books, Inventories and Capacity Utilisation Survey (OBICUS) for Q1:2026-27 reported aggregate manufacturing capacity utilisation at **74.6%** . This level lingers near the 75% threshold that industrial economists treat as the operational trigger for fresh private capex cycles. Until aggregate manufacturing utilisation breaches and sustains levels above 75-76%, industrial enterprises can easily service incremental demand by adjusting work shifts rather than constructing new production lines.


Operating capacity remains capped because broad-based consumption expenditure lacks momentum:


- **Consumption dominance:** Private Final Consumption Expenditure accounts for roughly **56% to 60% of GDP** , meaning national output is overwhelmingly consumption-driven.
- **Rural wage stagnation:** Labour Bureau data from the Wage Rates in Rural India series deflated by the Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Labourers reveals that **real rural wage growth** remained virtually stagnant or negative between 2019 and 2024.
- **Food inflation drag:** The Economic Survey confirmed that nominal rural wage growth failed to outpace elevated rural food inflation, leading to recurring spells of **negative real wage gains** for agricultural and casual non-farm labourers.


When the purchasing power of millions of rural households is eroded by inflation, demand for mass-market consumer durables and entry-level industrial goods inevitably contracts.

## Side-by-Side: Supply-Side Tax Breaks vs Wage-Led Demand Revival


Macroeconomic policymakers face a strategic choice between subsidising corporate capital inputs and regenerating bottom-up purchasing power. Supply-side interventions reduce the cost of capital, whereas wage-led strategies expand product markets via the accelerator principle, which posits that capital investment is induced by prior increases in output and consumption.


Evaluation Metric Supply-Side Tax Concessions (2019 Route) Wage-Led Demand Revival (Bottom-Up Route)


**Primary Statutory / Policy Mechanism** Sections 115BAA and 115BAB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 Rural safety nets (MGNREGS), real minimum wage enforcement, and MSME employment payroll support


**Direct Beneficiaries** Formal corporate enterprises, capital owners, and equity investors Agricultural labourers, informal wage earners, and rural households


**Corporate Balance Sheet Impact** Accelerated **balance sheet deleveraging**, liquid cash reserves, and higher dividend distributions Improved order book volumes, inventory liquidation, and elevated industrial capacity utilisation


**Output Multiplier Effect** Low immediate output multiplier due to high savings propensity among capital owners High fiscal multiplier of 2.45 to 3.25 from direct spending and consumption churn


**Fiscal Cost to Exchequer** Estimated at approximately ₹1.45 lakh crore annually in revenue foregone Reallocation of revenue expenditure towards targeted social transfers and rural capital works


**Capacity Utilisation Impact** Marginal; leaves factory utilisation idling near the **74.6% capacity threshold** Direct; absorbs idle manufacturing slack by expanding **Private Final Consumption Expenditure**


Econometric findings explain why corporate tax deductions produce limited immediate growth impulses. Working papers from the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy demonstrate that public capital outlays generate an **output multiplier of 2.45 to 3.25** , whereas untargeted corporate tax cuts yield significantly lower immediate output multipliers because windfalls leak into corporate savings.

## Fiscal Limits: Why Government Capex Cannot Carry the Burden Alone


The Central Government cannot indefinitely shoulder the entire burden of national capital formation without breaching statutory debt limits. Under the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management consolidation roadmap, the Centre committed to lowering its fiscal deficit below **4.5% of GDP** by FY 2025-26 while targeting a medium-term debt-to-GDP anchor of **50±1% by 2030-31** .


Rigid structural obligations restrict discretionary sovereign capital spending in two direct ways:


- **Heavy interest commitments:** Official expenditure profiles reveal that interest payments absorb **over 25% of general government** revenue and nearly 40% of the Centre's net revenue receipts, leaving narrow fiscal room to fund capital assets solely through market borrowing.
- **Macroeconomic trade-offs:** Expanding public capex in the absence of private participation threatens to crowd out private credit or precipitate ratings scrutiny.


Stagnant real rural wages suppress aggregate consumption, keeping factory operating rates below the private capex trigger threshold.


## Way Forward: Building Purchasing Power to Unlock Greenfield Investment


Industrial recovery requires an operational pivot from pure capital subsidisation toward reviving consumer purchasing power. NITI Aayog policy reviews and labour analyses suggest that industrial policy must complement capital support with targeted wage incentives, rural employment safety nets like MGNREGS, and credit backing for labour-intensive MSMEs.


A durable strategy for reviving private greenfield capex rests on three coordinated policy interventions:


1. **Restoring Rural Purchasing Power:** Real wage growth must be insulated from inflation through calibrated adjustments to minimum wages and enhanced rural infrastructure allocations, ensuring that rural real incomes support entry-level consumer goods manufacturing.
2. **Targeting Production Incentives to Employment:** Production-Linked Incentive schemes should be conditioned on verifiable domestic employment thresholds and domestic supply-chain integration rather than capital intensity alone.
3. **Formalising Informal Sector Productivity:** Expanding credit access and regulatory simplification for MSMEs will raise productivity and earnings across the informal economy, rebuilding the domestic customer base required to lift factory capacity utilisation safely past the 75% benchmark.

## Key Takeaways


- The Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 reduced corporate tax rates to 22% for existing companies and 15% for new manufacturing firms, resulting in an estimated annual revenue foregone of approximately ₹1.45 lakh crore.
- Corporate tax windfalls were predominantly deployed toward balance sheet deleveraging, debt reduction, and liquid cash accumulation rather than fresh greenfield assets, as documented by the Reserve Bank of India.
- Private corporate Gross Fixed Capital Formation has stagnated around 10-11% of GDP, far below its historical peak of 14-16% recorded in 2007-08 and 2011-12.
- Aggregate manufacturing capacity utilisation stood at 74.6% in Q1:2026-27 under the RBI OBICUS survey, remaining below the threshold required to trigger autonomous private capex cycles.
- Stagnant or negative real rural wage growth between 2019 and 2024 depressed Private Final Consumption Expenditure, which generates 56% to 60% of national GDP.
- Fiscal consolidation constraints under the FRBM framework, alongside interest payments consuming nearly 40% of net central revenue receipts, prevent the government from indefinitely funding public infrastructure outlays without private capex participation.
